Lessons.Title: How Would You Describe These Figures?
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 1 (2021): learn to notice, draw and describe geometric figures clearly to another person. Informal language is welcome. This lesson prepares for formal definitions of point, line and line segment in the NEXT lesson; learners need not formally distinguish an infinite line from a segment now.

Warm-up (5 minutes): discuss what you notice and wonder about a string-art arrangement. Name locations, directions and straight strokes, and make vague observations clearer. The publisher's third-party string-art photo is not reproduced.

Activity 1 (25 minutes): in pairs sit back to back; Partner A describes a source figure card without showing it, Partner B draws it. Compare the card and drawing, revise positional language and repeat. After two rounds, switch roles for two more. Teacher supplies legitimate original cards or separately designed first-party figures.

Activity 2 (15 minutes): use a straightedge and an isometric dot field. Draw FIVE straight lines, each passing through at least TWO dots and extending as far as possible; mark a familiar triangle, quadrilateral, letter or number made by parts of those lines. Share observations with classmates.

Synthesis (10 minutes): discuss useful directions such as left/right, horizontal/vertical, crosses, above, below and start/stop; introduce the phrase line segment informally for a shorter part of a longer line. First-party Cool-down: orally describe two crossing straight strokes and two labelled dots; partner redraws and teacher assesses clarity.

Digital Practice checks which of two independently authored descriptions is more precise. Original open-ended figures, drawing accuracy and peer communication remain teacher-reviewed; numeric Practice is not proof of source drawing fidelity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Precise position words
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point identifies a location in a drawing; words such as above, halfway, centre, left and right help another person locate it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Replace here/there with an identifiable dot, crossing or relative location.
KeyConcepts.Example: Mark the dot where a vertical stroke crosses a horizontal stroke.

KeyConcepts.Title: Describe straight strokes
KeyConcepts.Definition: An artist can describe a straight mark by its direction and the dots or intersections it goes through.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name horizontal, vertical, diagonal or the points it passes through before the partner draws.
KeyConcepts.Example: Draw one long straight stroke through two dots in the upper row.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parts of longer lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: A familiar figure may be traced using shorter portions of the long lines that cross a dot field.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Informally notice where the portion begins and ends; formal definitions are taught in the next lesson.
KeyConcepts.Example: Trace the three shorter pieces making a triangle from the five drawn long lines.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up: notice and describe
WorkedExamples.Question: A teacher displays string art made from straight strokes. How can a student make a vague observation about its marks more precise?
WorkedExamples.Method: Notice, name a visible feature, and say where it is.
Steps: Notice which straight strokes cross, which directions appear, and any visible points.
Replace a remark like 'there are lines over there' with a reference to a visible crossing or orientation.
Compare the observation with the actual displayed picture and revise it if needed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Open observations; teacher checks the actual source image and explanations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not a fixed answer key or machine-assessed source figure.

WorkedExamples.Title: Back-to-back reconstruction
WorkedExamples.Question: A partner must reproduce a hidden figure card from spoken directions. How can the description become more accurate?
WorkedExamples.Method: Start with reference points, relative positions and directions, then compare and revise.
Steps: Describe the first visible dot or corner relative to the card edges.
Tell the partner which direction a straight stroke goes and where it ends or crosses another stroke.
Compare the drawing with the card; replace one unclear phrase with specific location words and repeat with another card.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Partner's drawing and improved verbal instructions; teacher reviews all four partner-card rounds.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original cards and geometry descriptions require source/teacher observation, not numeric auto-grading.

WorkedExamples.Title: Five lines through a dot field
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw five long straight lines, each through at least two dots, and highlight a familiar shape created by parts of the lines.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a straightedge, then trace a recognizable figure.
Steps: Draw a straight extended line through at least two marked dots.
Repeat until you have five lines, each touching at least two dots.
Trace a shape, letter or numeral made by shorter pieces and explain which dots or crossings locate those pieces.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Five qualifying lines and a highlighted figure; open construction for teacher review.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks exact line count, straightness, minimum two dots, shape and student description.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying 'put it there' or 'draw a big shape' without indicating where.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A partner who cannot see the picture cannot locate or orient it accurately.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name an identifiable point, side of the card, relative location and the direction of a stroke.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Insisting that students must memorize formal line-versus-segment definitions during the first exploration.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 teacher preparation explicitly reserves formal definitions for the next lesson.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Invite informal talk about the parts of longer lines, start/stop locations and geometric descriptions. Formalize later.

SummaryPoints: Improve oral and written descriptions of where points and straight marks appear.
Use four partner-card rounds to compare, revise and repeat drawing instructions, with teacher guidance.
Draw five long straight lines through two or more dots each and trace one familiar figure.
Independent teacher-scored Cool-down and original protected source visuals are not machine graded.

Visuals.Title: First-party description-comparison example
Visuals.Description: A text-based comparative prompt, not a replacement for original publisher picture cards.
Visuals.PrimaryLabel: Which is clearer for a hidden drawing?
Visuals.SecondaryLabel: 1) Draw something here. 2) Draw a vertical straight stroke through point P.
Items: Specific: vertical direction and named point P.
Vague: no starting location or orientation.
Compare the verbal description and the final drawing.
SecondaryItems: Teacher checks the source partner-card comparison and isometric dot-field drawings.
